chunks.content: Key Points Introduction Expanding Influence of Real-World Data (RWD) in Chinese Healthcare Transformation Worldwide, the burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) is rising rapidly under the trend of population aging [ ]. China is also undergoing a fast epidemiological transition, with the burden of disease shifting from communicable diseases to NCDs. In 2021, China had 10.6 million deaths due to NCDs, accounting for 91% of all deaths [ ]. The transition of disease burden is creating substantial demand for high-quality care and innovative medical products for the global healthcare system. Simultaneously, governments must find cost-effective treatments and allocate medical resources more rationally due to unsustainable health expenditures. China’s healthcare system, mirroring global trends, encounters these challenges and has been pursuing transformation over the past decades [ ]. In this context, real-world evidence (RWE) is gaining wide attention due to its value in informing resource allocation and facilitating fast regulatory and policy decisions [ ]. It has great potential to not only address proactive screening, early diagnosis, ambitious guidelines adoption at practice level and improve health outcomes as a result, but also steer global healthcare systems in a more patient-centered and cost-effective direction. As the core of generating RWE, real-world data (RWD) is continually demonstrating its impact, becoming a lifeblood of healthcare transformation. In 2016, the Chinese national government released the "Healthy China 2030" strategy, placing health at the center of all policies and proposing ambitious reforms that profoundly impact the healthcare system [ ]. As part of the journey towards healthcare transformation in China, the application of RWD/RWE is expanding. First, RWD/RWE is critical for public health policy planning and implementation. Given that the “Healthy China 2030” blueprint emphasizes chronic disease prevention and aims to reduce premature mortality [ ], national-level data platforms integrating multi-source RWD can help estimate population health indicators. Second, RWD/RWE addresses research questions throughout medical product life cycles, especially post-marketing safety surveillance. For example, based on RWD, China has developed the China Hospital Pharmacovigilance System (CHPS) [ ] and an active vaccine safety surveillance platform demonstrated in Ningbo [ , ]. Third, RWD/RWE can transform clinical practice by elucidating patient profiles, supporting diagnoses, describing treatment patterns, investigating prognostic factors, and improving clinical guidelines (Fig. ) [ ]. The benefits are not limited to these; as a vital complement to evidence from randomized controlled trials, RWE’s value continues to be uncovered in diverse areas. Activated Public–Private Partnership in China As RWD and RWE gain influence, discussions in China have attracted participants from government, universities, research institutions, and industry. The Chinese healthcare system has the wealth, technology, capacity and know-how to set and pursue a bolder aspiration for our health, by unlocking the potential of the systematic, equitable, and extensive application of existing RWD. Recent workshops and scientific committees focusing on RWD and RWE have been initiated to foster collaborative relationships and amplify the impact of Chinese RWE globally [ ]. These workshops have established a vision of RWE transforming the future of healthcare in China and identified several RWD-related challenges, including limited data access and sharing, difficulties in cross-system data integration, lack of high-quality data, and the absence of unified and standardized data curation processes [ – ]. Despite the identification of these challenges, it remains unclear whether the current healthcare environment in China has the capacity to address these issues. Moreover, it is unknown what the necessary steps are that the Chinese RWE community needs to take towards this goal. To address these, in-depth interviews and a roundtable workshop with experts were conducted to generate insights. This article synthesizes expert insights and discussions, structured from the following aspects: assessing China’s capacity and potential opportunities to address existing challenges, summarizing key milestones toward achieving high-quality RWD and RWE, and recommending how various healthcare stakeholders can take action to foster a data-driven, integrated, resilient healthcare system with the patient at the center. By reimagining evidence generation together, we build, align and expand RWD capabilities; connect healthcare players by RWD partnerships and healthcare ecosystems/platforms; understand unmet healthcare needs and identify high-risk patients; deliver practice defining RWE. Situation Assessments of RWD Development The development of RWE in China is at a critical juncture, urgently requiring a breakthrough to fix current bottlenecks faced by RWD. With a wealth of successful cases and practical experiences accumulated over the past several years in China, significant opportunities present themselves. We attempt to analyze this from the perspectives of macro-level policies, a comprehensive guideline system, innovative tools and methods, and professional knowledge. We attempt to analyze this from the perspectives of macro-level policies, a comprehensive guideline system, innovative tools and methods, and professional knowledge. Supportive Policy Environment The “Healthy China 2030” blueprint has identified the prevention and treatment of diseases and the improvement of population health as a national goal [ ], which has greatly driven the demand for data in clinical and public health fields. In this context, the government has invested in numerous cohort studies, greatly enriching available RWD sources in China. As of 2019, China had over 300 published natural population cohorts and disease-specific cohorts [ ]. One of the most representative cohort studies is the China Kadoorie Biobank (CKB), which covers more than 500,000 healthy adults across ten provinces and has a follow-up period of nearly 20 years [ ]. To enhance cohort data information sharing and collaboration, a platform called the China Cohort Consortium (CCC), covering the information of 145 cohorts, was also established in 2017 [ ]. In addition, as an important action stressed in the "Healthy China 2030" plan, China has established 488 national-level and 807 provincial-level comprehensive prevention and control demonstration areas for chronic diseases [ ]. These demonstration areas focus on conducting early screening and health management for residents and promoting information connectivity across medical and public health institutions. These efforts have been generating substantial RWD, such as health monitoring data and physical examination data. Another national data strategy is the “National Plan for the Layout of Digital China" released in 2023 [ ], which emphasizes strengthening data infrastructure, promoting the collection and utilization of public data, and establishing national databases for public health. In the era of Digital China, it is expected that Chinese RWD will be more abundant, accessible, and regulated. With the support of open national strategies, regional policies have begun piloting support for RWD development as well. As a great example, the Boao Lecheng pilot zone in Hainan province established an RWD platform to collect the clinical records of the pre-authorized use of pharmaceutical products and medical devices [ , ]. This platform documents precious real-world use data of medical products urgently needed in clinical practice. As collection, curation, and management strictly adhere to the released RWD guidelines, these data can satisfy the requirements of drug registration studies. This provides an important model for the governance of high-quality RWD platforms in China. In addition, Hainan Province is also piloting the integration of data from medical institutions, health insurance, and drug regulatory systems, which has created approximately nine million interconnected health records [ ]. Evolving Guideline System While supportive policies have created the demand and environment for RWD development, effectively transforming RWD into high-quality RWE requires the guidance of actionable frameworks. China’s real-world study (RWS) guideline system is continuously evolving and aligning with global regulatory advancements. Global interest in leveraging RWD and RWE to support regulatory decision making for drugs and medical devices is growing. The United States, Europe, the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, and China have released technical guidelines on RWS [ ]. Recently, the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) released the first global guideline draft on utilizing RWD for drug safety assessment [ ], marking a new milestone in global regulatory science with RWS. Since joining the ICH in 2017, China has established a world-leading RWS guideline system (Fig. ) [ , ]. Led by these guidelines, China has made extensive explorations of applying RWE in various aspects. In particular, the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) has accumulated a wealth of practical experience in RWE supporting regulatory decision making for medical products, resulting in successful cases of new drug and device registrations, indication approvals, label expansions, and safety modifications [ ]. By the end of 2023, 13 healthcare products were approved for marketing through the Boao Lecheng pilot zone [ ]. China’s RWS guideline system is relatively comprehensive, but still evolving with updates for guidelines on common RWS data sources and specific RWD application areas. For example, in 2023, the NMPA drafted a guideline on disease registries [ ], a data source with unique value for RWS of rare diseases. In 2024, the NMPA released the latest guideline on using RWD to support proactive drug safety monitoring [ ], which provides a significant reference for the development of a national RWD-based active pharmacovigilance system. In 2024, the NMPA released the latest guideline on using RWD to support proactive drug safety monitoring [ ], which provides a significant reference for the development of a national RWD-based active pharmacovigilance system. Data Foundation and Tools Solid Data Foundation China’s immense population provides a wealth of clinical and public health data, presenting unique opportunities for generating RWE. Nowadays, many existing data sources have gradually matured while new RWD sources continue to emerge. However, researchers have not yet fully integrated and utilized the potential of these data sources (Fig. ). In terms of clinical data, China has seen a surge in disease registries and databases targeting specific diseases. As an example, the Guangzhou Institute of Respiratory Health collaborated with 33 hospitals nationwide to conduct the first severe asthma registry study in China (C-BIOPRED) [ ]. This registry revealed the unmet treatment needs of Chinese patients with severe asthma and provided rich clinical characteristic data. Similarly, in response to the high prevalence of chronic kidney disease in China, the China Renal Data System (CRDS) has been established, which now covers clinical data of kidney patients from 24 hospitals [ ]. Based on this database, researchers have successfully produced high-quality RWE with global impact [ ]. Public health data is an important complement to clinical data. The China Chronic Disease and Risk Factors Surveillance study is a nationwide cross-sectional study conducted every 3 years since 2004, covering 170 million people across 31 provinces, collecting data on common chronic diseases, risk factors, physical measurements, and routine laboratory tests, which has unique value for generating RWE [ ]. Another resource is China’s national mortality surveillance system, which provides total and cause-specific mortality data and plays a crucial role in assessing the impact of policies, interventions, and treatment strategies on mortality [ ]. Innovative Digital Intelligent Solutions While China possesses abundant RWD sources, their heterogeneity and fragmented distribution hinder the full realization of their research potential. Consequently, fostering the integration of complex data sources and creating data platforms is an essential path for leveraging RWD effectively in China. Currently, several technological and methodological solutions for promoting data platforms have been explored, with corresponding practical cases of implementation. The integration of RWD data sources refers to two dimensions. The first dimension is the cross-institutional data integration of the same type of RWD (e.g., electronic health records [EHR]). The major challenge lies in limited exchangeability due to the heterogeneous terminologies, formats, and structures of different institutions. The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) common data model (CDM), an open community data standard, was designed to address this issue [ ]. In China, OMOP is used not only to integrate EHR but also to integrate cohort data. For example, researchers from Peking University have established a large-scale respiratory disease cohort based on five mature community cohorts and four clinical disease cohorts in China [ ]. The second dimension of integration is the linkage of various types of RWD sources, which helps to obtain life-course health data. As an innovative case, the Chinese Medical Association (CMA) and the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC) are piloting the linkage of the Chinese Medicine Clinical Case Repository (CMCR) database with the national death registration data to create a clinical disease-specific cohort database. The case report data primarily serve as valuable resources for physician training and experience sharing. By combining these with death registry data, their application will be further expanded to investigate the survival outcomes and prognostic factors influencing these outcomes by conducting RWS. Confidentiality concerns often pose barriers to data sharing. Federated networks (FN) analysis offers a solution by allowing data to remain within the institution’s information system while still supporting collaborative research [ ]. In this model, researchers can send analysis codes to the participating institutions remotely, and only the aggregated results, not patient-level data, are returned, ensuring privacy. This decentralized technology is increasingly used in China. The ultimate goal of RWD integration in China is to establish a national-level health data ecosystem. Leveraging the opportunities mentioned above, Shandong Province has issued policy and piloted the establishment of the National Health and Medical Big Data Center (North) [ ]. One of the remarkable fruits of this center is the Cheeloo Lifespan Electronic Health Research Data Library (Cheeloo LEAD) [ ]. Using CDM and FN, Cheeloo LEAD integrates data from 5,152,597 individuals across 4909 hospitals and primary healthcare institutions in 39 urban areas of Shandong Province, China, with a follow-up period of approximately 14 years. The data encompasses demographic information, diseases, medications, laboratory tests, and surgical records. This foundation provides high-quality data for RWS and offers valuable experience for the development of a national-level data platform in the future. Growing RWD Talents In

Using CDM and FN, Cheeloo LEAD integrates data from 5,152,597 individuals across 4909 hospitals and primary healthcare institutions in 39 urban areas of Shandong Province, China, with a follow-up period of approximately 14 years. The data encompasses demographic information, diseases, medications, laboratory tests, and surgical records. This foundation provides high-quality data for RWS and offers valuable experience for the development of a national-level data platform in the future. Growing RWD Talents In previous discussions about the development of RWD and RWE, the importance of talent has often been overlooked. As China experiences rapid growth in RWD and RWE, it is crucial to recognize and address the increasing demand for skilled professionals in this field. Currently, some universities are creating interdisciplinary RWD talent programs. For example, the Medical Dataology major at Shandong University offers education in medicine, epidemiology, mathematics, and computer science, preparing talents for RWS [ ]. The healthcare industry is also collaborating with academia to enhance talent reserves. Universities provide expertise, while the industry offers RWS project opportunities. For instance, AstraZeneca (AZ) and Peking University (PKU) Health Science Center jointly established the PKU-AZ RWE Research Laboratory [ ], allowing students to participate in RWS projects in pharmaceutical companies. At the same time, utilizing this RWS platform, AZ and PKU jointly generated high-quality RWE to enrich evidence-based medicine and advance chronic disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. Roadmap for Advancing High-Quality RWD/RWE in China The conducive policy environment, comprehensive guideline system, innovative methodologies, and robust talent pool have laid a solid foundation for the development of RWD and RWE in China. Moving forward, it is necessary to outline a clear roadmap for building high-quality RWD sources and harmonizing RWE generation in the future (Fig. ). Construction of Nationwide RWD Sources To achieve the goal of lowering premature mortality due to chronic diseases in the “Healthy China 2030” blueprint [ ], the Chinese government has launched targeted prevention and control programs for four major types of chronic disease: cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes mellitus [ ]. Recognizing that various RWD sources play diverse roles in supporting national health strategies, we set specific development goals based on the types of data sources. Currently, besides the integrated platform for the burden of chronic disease study [ ], several cities in China have achieved health data interoperability by establishing regional health data platforms. The next crucial step is to integrate these into a national health data platform within the next 5 years (i.e., national public health data collaborative innovation initiatives and special disease cohorts). This national platform will serve as a powerful tool for understanding the disease spectrum, assessing key epidemiological and disease burden indicators, and evaluating the impact of policies and interventions, at both national and regional levels. To build this platform, it is essential to establish unified data standards and address technical barriers. China’s previous experience in designing an integrated data platform for chronic diseases will provide valuable reference [ ]. Meanwhile, a data-sharing mechanism will be developed to facilitate different users and stakeholders in conducting RWS and promoting data utilization. In addition to measuring health indicators, RWD guiding disease control and prevention to improve population health is fundamental. Disease registries and natural-population cohorts can exert synergistic effects in this aspect. Currently, China’s disease registries exhibit significant variability in quality, with a notable shortage of registries possessing large sample sizes. In the future, China needs to establish larger-scale and higher-quality disease registries, particularly targeting high-burden chronic diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, and COPD. Based on the data from these registries, clinical decision support systems can be developed to rapidly generate evidence and guide clinical practice, thereby achieving data-driven improvements in the quality of care. Establishing a disease registry involves planning and design, database construction, data access, entry, quality control, and database integration and expansion. The recently released disease registry guidelines in 2023 provide detailed guidance for this process [ ]. Different from the role of disease registries, natural-population cohorts can help identify risk factors for disease occurrence, thereby identifying priorities for disease prevention. In the future, more nationwide natural-population cohorts are expected to be established by integrating various existing data sources, including national cross-sectional survey data, hospital discharge records, and death registry data. Data standardization is crucial for health data integration. Chinese researchers have the most experience with OMOP-CDM, while many other CDMs have been well developed globally, such as Informatics for Integrating Biology and the Bedside (i2b2) CDM, and Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Network (PCORnet) CDM [ ]. Data standardization is crucial for health data integration. Chinese researchers have the most experience with OMOP-CDM, while many other CDMs have been well developed globally, such as Informatics for Integrating Biology and the Bedside (i2b2) CDM, and Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Network (PCORnet) CDM [ ]. However, the architecture design and terminology standards of international CDMs cannot be perfectly employed in China’s application scenarios. A key future objective will be to establish a nationwide Chinese data standard by extending international CDMs based on the characteristics of Chinese medical data. Harmonization of the RWE Community As China progresses in the development of RWD, some additional efforts are also necessary to ensure the harmonious generation of RWE. Over the next few years, China needs to establish a national-level RWE expert committee. This committee will serve as a think tank, including experts with diverse academic backgrounds. The committee will be responsible for regularly collecting feedback and updating guidelines, providing professional guidance by issuing expert consensus, enhancing the exchange of cutting-edge knowledge, and improving public awareness and acceptance for RWE by organizing academic conferences. In the future, more extensive public–private partnerships will be established among industry, academia, and research institutes to create a positive RWE ecosystem in China. Regarding talent development, universities and industry will engage in deep collaboration to cultivate excellent talents with practical skills. The forms of collaboration can be diverse, including internship programs, university-enterprise joint training programs, and post-doctoral workstations in enterprises. In terms of research collaboration, a nationwide RWE innovative laboratory will be established. Industries, academia, and institutions can use this platform to share resources and collaboratively produce internationally influential RWE based on their project opportunities. Call for Action: Future Efforts to Build an RWE Ecosystem in China China has a well-defined future roadmap for leveraging RWE to transform medical practice and is taking a step-by-step approach to achieve this goal. To conclude, the short-term goal is to actively engage multiple stakeholders, fully integrate existing resources, and establish sustainable private–public partnerships. A key outcome at this stage will be the preliminary establishment of a national-level RWD platform, covering data from many pilot regions with geographical representativeness. To expand the platform’s influence and coverage, the mid-term goal is to fully utilize the platform to conduct high-quality research and produce internationally impactful RWE. Throughout this process, more participants will be attracted to join and collectively expand the platform. Meanwhile, data governance capabilities and data quality can be enhanced by substantial data usage. After overcoming data bottlenecks, our long-term goal will no longer be limited to data construction but instead will be to unlock the potential of RWE to drive patient-centered transformation in China’s healthcare. A nationwide RWD platform will become a powerful tool, and the established partnership foundation will continue to benefit the integration and generation of more high-quality RWD sources, continuously serving this long-term mission. With the guarantee of policies, guidelines, methods, and talents, China is fully prepared to achieve the ambitious goals set for the next few decades. However, to complete this mission, all healthcare stakeholders must collaborate to build a patient-centered ecosystem, fully utilizing RWD and RWE opportunities. As a call for action, several suggestions are provided in Table for key stakeholders, including government, regulatory authorities, industry, academia, clinical researchers and institutions, and data service providers, for consideration. Conclusion A new data-driven, patient-centered, collaborative healthcare ecosystem is on the rise in China. This article explored the current state and potential of RWD/RWE development within the context of the “Healthy China 2030” initiative, examining key areas including policy environment, guideline systems, data infrastructure, and talent development. The assessment reveals that China has significant potential to leverage current resources and opportunities to advance high-quality RWD/RWE development. We also outlined a roadmap for the long-term goal of achieving RWE-transforming patient-centered healthcare in China, which emphasizes the construction of nationwide RWD resources and harmonization of RWE generation through public–private partnerships. As a call to action for various healthcare stakeholders including government, regulatory authorities, industry, academia, clinical researchers, and data service providers, we underscored the collaborative effort to create a robust RWE ecosystem and provided several specific suggestions. Unlocking RWE’s power to transform the care of millions of people living with chronic diseases in China requires extensive participation from stakeholders.
